title: Re-evaluating your dog’s diet
publisher: Cornell University College of Veterinary Medicine — Riney Canine Health Center
topic: dog nutrition, treats, home-prepared diets, and diet transitions
geographicScope: General canine nutrition education; product labels and nutrition standards can vary by country.
content:
A dog’s main food should provide complete and balanced nutrition for the dog’s life stage. Owners considering a home-prepared diet should work with a board-certified veterinary nutritionist so the recipe supplies the necessary nutrients.

Treats and table scraps can displace balanced nutrition and add substantial calories. Cornell advises being conservative with treats; using a portion of the dog’s regular daily food for rewards can help keep intake balanced.

Home-prepared diets can be deficient in important nutrients when they are not professionally formulated. Meat-heavy recipes are not automatically complete, and dogs with health conditions may need a plan designed by a veterinary nutritionist.

Chicken and rice or another bland diet may be useful only temporarily for digestive upset, but it is not nutritionally balanced for long-term feeding. Repeated or persistent stomach problems need veterinary assessment rather than repeated long-term bland feeding.

Cornell describes a four-day food transition for most dogs: 75% old food and 25% new food on the first day, equal portions on the second day, 25% old food and 75% new food on the third day, and only the new food on the fourth day. Dogs with sensitive stomachs may need a longer, more gradual change. Diarrhea lasting more than a day or two, or diarrhea accompanied by other symptoms, warrants contacting a veterinarian.
